newsitem.title: USA: RJR papers to be introduced in tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: RJR papers to be introduced in tobacco case.

text.p: A 1962 document that a researcher says contains "overwhelming" evidence of the health hazards of cigarette smoke is to be offered as evidence in a Florida tobacco trial in April, a lawyer said on Thursday.

The document demonstrates that the R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co knew the hazards of cigarette smoke in the early 1960s and failed to act to correct a defective product, said Stephanie Hartley, an associate of Jacksonville lawyer Norwood Wilner.
Wilner has filed several hundred product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against tobacco companies.
Wilner's office released the document on Thursday and said it would be on a witness and evidence list to be submitted Friday for the April 7 trial of a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds.

A spokeswoman for R.J. Reynolds said the document was not a secret, having been introduced in litigation eight times in the past 12 years, and was being used by Wilner to prejudice the jury pool in advance of the trial.

In the lawsuit, plaintiff Dana Raulerson contends that Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp knew cigarettes were dangerous. Raulerson filed the suit as a representative of the estate of her sister, Jean Connor, a smoker who filed a product liability suit against Reynolds in March 1995, but died of lung cancer that fall.
Last month, Duval Circuit Judge Bernard Nachman ruled that Raulerson can ask a jury to award punitive damages.

Hartley said the document, written in 1962 by R.J. Reynolds research scientist Alan Rodgman, supported the claim by anti- tobacco litigators that cigarette companies have long known the danger of cigarette smoke and failed to do anything about it.
"Obviously, the amount of evidence accumulated to indict cigarette smoke as a health hazard is overwhelming. The evidence challenging such an indictment is scant," Rodgman wrote.
"That tells us that they knew cigarettes were a health hazard," Hartley said. "Legally, upon a showing like that, they should have done something. They needed to warn the consumers."
R.J. Reynolds spokeswoman Peggy Carter said the document was a draft memorandum that simply summarized the scientific findings of the day.

In a statement, the company said Reynolds had "actively participated in the efforts to better understand the issues associated with smoking" and Wilner's release of the document was an attempt to influence prospective jurors in the Raulerson case.
"Mr. Wilner is just a few weeks away from walking into a courtroom. This is clearly an attempt to prejudice the jury pool...and he has left out quite a few details," Carter said.
Rodgman also wrote that members of the RJR research department had "studied in detail cigarette smoke composition."
"However, much data remain unpublished because they are concerned with carcinogenic or cocarcinogenic compounds," he wrote.
Hartley said that statement indicated that Reynolds had engaged in a cover-up of the effects of cigarette smoke.
"It tells us they are suppressing important data that the public needs to know, and they are doing it because they know cigarettes are carcinogenic," she said.
